new_statements.quote: The phonological word in Khmu consists of one, two or three syllables. The stress occurs on the main final syllable of the word. The majority of words are monosyllabic or disyllabic (sesquisyllabic). The presyllable C(C)V(C) of disyllabic words is unstressed and the vowel is just a transitional or reduced vowel. Examples from an EK dialect is provided.

new_statements.second_reader_evidence: QUOTE: Opened (page scan of Premsrirat 2004, MKS 34, p. 10) and the scanned the text. Under the heading '2) Syllables and word structure of Khmu' the page reads exactly: 'The phonological word in Khmu consists of one, two or three syllables. The stress occurs on the main final syllable of the word. The majority of words are monosyllabic or disyllabic (sesquisyllabic). The presyllable C(C)ᵛ(C) of disyllabic words is unstressed and the vowel is just a transitional or reduced vowel. Examples from an EK dialect is provided.' (only difference from the report: the presyllable vowel is printed as a superscript V). The examples (h'm'ma:l 'soul', tᶜla:m'pa:m 'butterfly' etc., stress mark before the…
new_statements.rule_in_words: Khmu words (1-3 syllables, mostly mono- or sesquisyllabic) carry a single stress on the final (main) syllable; presyllables are unstressed with a reduced/transitional vowel, and in the tonal Western Khmu varieties (incl. ct = Om Kae, Sipsongpanna) the presyllable is often deleted altogether. This is a statement about Khmu generally (seven dialects, two of them in Sipsongpanna, China), applied to kuan1250 only under Glottolog's hypothesis that 'Kuanhua' is Khmu spoken in Jinghong.
new_statements.secondary_stress: None mentioned; presyllables described as unstressed (no secondary stress).
new_statements.exceptions: None for stress placement. Trisyllables C(C)V(C).CV(C).'C(C)V(C) also final-stressed (examples tᶜlaːm'paːm 'butterfly', kᶜldɔŋ'dɛːŋ 'firefly'). WK tonal dialects ct/lb delete the presyllable, yielding monosyllables.
new_statements.domain_note: Phonological word, citation forms; statement is pan-dialectal for Khmu (EK and WK), with data from fieldwork 1996-2002 incl. two villages in Sipsongpanna (Yunnan). NOT a description of 'Kuanhua' by name — see the note on which variety.
new_statements.identity_note: kuan1250 'Kuanhua' is a Glottolog bookkeeping (retired) languoid with zero descriptive references; ISO xnh is still active. Ethnologue (E17, source EDCL 1991) itself says the speakers in Jinghong are 'locally considered part of Khmu peoples', and Glottolog (after Svantesson p.c. 2011) reads Kuan < kwɛɛn (Khmu Khuen/Kween ethnonym, cf. khue1238) and Damai < tmɔɔi 'subgroup', i.e. probably just Khmu [kjg, khmu1256] on the Chinese side; Wikipedia reports Li Yunbing 2005 instead classing 宽语 as 'Mangic' (unverified, print only). The quoted statement is Premsrirat's pan-dialect description of Khmu (khmu1256), whose sample includes two Sipsongpanna villages (Pung Soa = Eastern Khmu, Om Kae = tonal Western Khmu) but no variety named Kuan/Khuen in Jinghong. Khmu khmu1256 is already in the current catalog (StressTyp2, final stress, verified-clean), so cataloguing kuan1250 separately on this evidence would double-count one entity; hence not proposed for the catalog.

new_statements.quote: A minor syllable is a short, unstressed syllables preceding the major syllable of a word. The vowel of a minor syllable is a syllabic nasal or liquid, or a shwa-vowel, which is not indicated in our transcriptions. [p. 49] ... Most Kammu words consist of one major syllable, or a major syllable preceded by a minor syllable. Major syllables have the structure C(C)V(C). [p. 46] ... The northern dialects (Yuan, Khween, Rook, Kroong, Lii) have almost identical phoneme systems, in which the feature 'voice' plays only a minor role. In these dialects there are two distinctive tones, 'high' and 'low'. [p. 46] ... In Northern Kammu some words have a distinctive contrast between a high falling tone and a low even tone ... while in most words tone is no distinctive feature. [p. 47]

new_statements.relation_note: Same placement as the existing Premsrirat 2004 statement (stress on the main/final syllable, presyllable unstressed): Lindell et al. state it from the other side (the minor syllable is unstressed; word = (minor)+major). It refines by adding the two-tone contrast of Northern Kammu (Khween included) and by covering the Khween tmooy, which is the variety Glottolog's comment ties to 'Kuan'. The stress placement itself is stated indirectly (where stress is absent, not where it falls).
new_statements.rule_in_words: Words are one major syllable optionally preceded by a minor (pre-)syllable; the minor syllable is short and unstressed, so prominence sits on the major syllable, which is always word-final. Northern Kammu (incl. Khween) additionally has a marginal high/low tone contrast on some major syllables (a reflex of the old voicing contrast); Southern Kammu (Uu) has no tone.
new_statements.exceptions: None on stress. On tone: only some words carry the high/low contrast in Northern Kammu; the tone contrast is 'redundant' in the Uu speaker if initial voicing is taken as primary.
new_statements.identity_note: The work describes Kammu (Khmu) dialects of Northern Laos by tmooy: Yuan (Y), Khween (Kh), Rook (R1, R2), Kroong (Kr), Lii (L) = Northern Kammu, and Uu (U) = Southern Kammu. It does not mention Kuanhua, Kuan, Damai, Jinghong or China-side speakers by name. Its relevance to kuan1250 rests on Glottolog's (Svantesson p.c. 2011) reading of 'Kuan' as the Khween/Kween tmooy of Khmu, which this article covers with two Khween word-list speakers; the p. 49 statement is given as holding 'in all dialects'.
